newsitem.title: UK: Subdued dlr fails to capitalise from U.S. air raid.
newsitem.headline: Subdued dlr fails to capitalise from U.S. air raid.

text.p: The dollar closed lower against the mark and held steady against the yen after a brief spike higher on news of U.S. military intervention in Iraq failed to spark follow-through buying, dealers said.

The dollar erased all its intraday gains as interest rate concerns took centre-stage again, stoked by an article in the Wall Street Journal that said the Federal Reserve was moving towards a larger-than-expected rate rise.
"For the currency markets, the Iraq story proved to be a bit of a non-event," said Julian Jessop at Nikko Europe.
At 1440 GMT, the dollar was at 1.4840/50 marks and 109.25/33 yen, off session highs of 1.4912 and 109.45. That compared to 1.4863/70 and 109.10/18 at Monday's European close.

U.S. President Bill Clinton extended the no-fly zone in southern Iraq to Baghdad's southern suburbs after the U.S. launched a cruise missile attack on Iraq in retaliation for Iraq's military move against the Kurds.

"For the dollar to gain more support from this, the whole thing would have to spill over outside Iraq, and it doesn't seem that Clinton would want to do anything that will blow up in his face," said Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko.
Given the poor state of the Iraqi armed forces, analysts saw little threat that the situation would escalate.

Even though oil prices spiked to their highest level since the Gulf War, hitting $23.50 per barrel, the dollar's response was fairly muted amid concern the inflationary implications of higher oil prices might spook the bond markets.
"...the positive effects for the dollar are being diluted by the potentially negative response of the bond market," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Equally, the bond market's dislike of rising interest rates, also tended to hurt the dollar, said Meggyesi.

Dollar/yen held steady as yen selling was more pronounced on the crosses, where it fell to a seven-week low against the mark at 73.67 and also hit seven-week lows against sterling at 171.30 yen. The yen is vulnerable to higher oil prices because of Japan's dependency on oil imports.
Apart from short-lived upward spikes the dollar has not managed to sustain its gains from similar situations in the past, analysts said.
After the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, oil prices jumped to a high of over $40 a barrel and the dollar gained almost two pfennigs in the two days after the takeover.
In the following two weeks the dollar lost five pfennigs, and as oil prices subsided from their peak, the dollar resumed its slide to below 1.50 marks by early 1991.

The dollar shrugged off the National Association of Purchasing Management report for August which was broadly in line with expectations at 52.6, up from 50.2 in July. The main focus remains U.S. jobs data for August due on Friday.

Interest rate rise speculation was stoked by an article in the Wall Street Journal which said the Federal Reserve was moving towards a sharper-than-expected rate increase unless clear signs of slower growth appeared in the next three weeks.
The next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee is on September 24.
Peripheral European currencies and the French franc gained some relief from the Iraqi news. Currencies associated with oil price swings, such as sterling, notched up gains.
The pound hit 9-1/2 week highs against the dollar just shy of $1.57 and reached seven-week peaks against the mark at 2.3293 marks.
